newsitem.title: USA: TWA sees quarter hurt by crash, fuel costs.
newsitem.headline: TWA sees quarter hurt by crash, fuel costs.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc.'s third-quarter results are expected to reflect the financial toll taken by the explosion of Flight 800 off the coast of New York's Long Island as well as rising fuel costs and scheduling mishaps.

The St. Louis-based carrier Wednesday confirmed predictions by some Wall Street analysts that it will face some short-term pressure on profits, with third-quarter results anticipated to fall below last year's levels.
But analysts said July's crash only compounded other problems.
"I'm not so sure the lion's share of the problems is attributable to the crash," said Edward Starkman, an industry analyst and editor of The Starkman Airline Report.
Starkman said the company had "significant problems in summer scheduling," due, in part, to a delayed delivery of some aircraft that were being refurbished.
"In a summer when you're seeing some peak (travel volume) levels, not being able to get those planes flying can really hurt you," he said.
TWA had expected to build up service by 13 percent in the third quarter to take advantage of peak summer travel.

But the plane delivery delays and the loss of Flight 800 caused TWA to fall short of those goals, analysts said. Profits were also hurt by the costs of trying to implement an aggressive growth plan, analysts said.

The aircraft exploded in mid-air without warning just 11-1/2 minutes after taking off from New York's Kennedy airport on a flight to Paris and its wreckage was strewn over a wide area off the small town of East Moriches on New York's Long Island. The bodies or remains of 213 victims have been recovered.

Lead investigators said at a news conference Monday that none of the three theories on the cause of the aircraft explosion on July 17 had been ruled out. These included a bomb, a missile or catastrophic mechanical failure.
TWA noted that it suffered more than some rivals did from fuel cost increases because its fleet -- one of the oldest among U.S. carriers -- is less fuel-efficient.
TWA said its international bookings declined after the crash of the Boeing 747 jetliner July 17. Still, summer traffic volumes, load factors and total revenues exceeded last year's levels, it said.

TWA said it saw "a slight temporary falloff in advance bookings ... (resulting) in September passenger loads that are below expectations." The airline said it has not observed any drop in advance bookings for Ocotber and later.

"Operationally and emotionally, this has been an extremely difficult summer for the people of TWA, and unfortunately it now appears that we will see these difficulties reflected in third-quarter results," said Chief Executive Jeffrey Erickson.

TWA remains on track to complete the turnaround it began when it emerged from a second bankruptcy in August 1995, analysts said, but the carrier still has some operational problems, including an ageing fleet and out-of-date technology.

"They're still moving in the right direction ... the question is whether they are moving fast enough ... to get the job done before the next downturn in the industry," said Lehman Brothers analyst Brian Harris.
